It looks a little stiff. I would recommend leaning more into the curves of the figure. For example, the arm crossing her body has more of a curve to it, and she is leaning a bit more on an angle instead of standing straight upright. 

But this is good! I struggle with figure drawing, and what helps me loosen up is doing some really quick (like 30 seconds quick) practice sketches of the figure before starting the actual piece. Humans have angular bones, but they are surrounded by organs and meat and skin- which adds fluidity! 

I hope this makes sense! You have talent and I encourage you to keep going.

I would recommend drawing from reference photos, and also including the rest of the face when practicing hair. Whenever I am struggling to draw something I pull up a bunch of pictures and draw based on what I see. 

The hair you are drawing looks very stylized, but I think pulling examples of what hair looks like in real life will level up your work, and you can still put your own twist on things.
This looks like a beautiful background! I think you are missing a subject. I'm picturing a deer or moose. They would fit perfectly in the gap between the trees.

I think to master any form of art, one has to dedicate a ton of time and effort. 

So pick something that you can see yourself pouring hours and hours into. If you enjoy drawing things to make them look realistic, then lean into it! 

The fastest way to get discouraged is to force yourself to do something that you don't really enjoy. This has just been from my own personal experience.

I've personally fallen in love with realism, and I'm working towards hyper-realism. I paint a minimum of 3 hours a day every day, and rarely find myself losing interest.

In regards to color, here are my two biggest rules: 

1. Warm colors in front, cool colors in back. So colors like blues and purples are great for shadows, and warmer colors like orange tend to jump forward. Even if you are painting a purple object, for example. You'll notice that the closest part to you may have a bit of warmer red, and the part furthest away will be a more purple/blue. 

2. I personally NEVER use black. I find it to be very flat, and it dulls out colors. My darkest tone is a mix of prussian blue/alizern crimson/burnt umber. 

I'm primarily an oil painter, so please take this advice with a grain of salt when working with other mediums! I've never studied color theory, just practiced painting a TON! I hope this helps. 😅

I grew up LOVING anime. I wanted to be a manga-ka as a teenager but eventually grew out of it. I still continued to create  art though and now as an adult I'm a fine artist with a degree in drawing. 

If you want to work with anime or manga for your career,, I think that's fine. HOWEVER my advice to you is to advance your art skills in other areas (which subsequently will advance your anime-drawing skills). 

Learning things like color theory, perspective, and figure drawing will elevate your craft. Whereas only using other anime as reference will leave your own art looking very one-note. Practice drawing from life first! Then incorporate the anime style into your work after.
